statutes_cited: Section 54 of The Land Acquisition Act, 1894
Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894
holding: Further, the Supreme Court of Pakistan in paragraph 17 of the judgment ibid explained why the entire area, and not its parts, is the unit of valuation in a single project acquisition and held that “where land is acquired for one project, the potential value of the entire area being acquired is relevant as the very purpose of the acquisition suggests that the land has future prospects.” Likewise, the review filed by the Federal Government against aforesaid judgment (PLD 2023 Supreme Court 277) was dismissed by the Supreme Court of Pakistan through judgment “FEDERAL GOVERNMENT OF PAKISTAN through Ministry of Defence Rawalpindi and others versus Mst. ZAKIA BEGUM and others” (2023 SCMR 2092) holding as under: “Considering that the land is acquired for a single project, this Court has affirmed the value assigned by the High Court to the acquired land for the reason that the original value as determined by the Collector and the Referee Court was based on revenue classifications which have no relevance for the purposes of calculating compensation. Furthermore, when land is acquired in small parcels, awarding compensation based on revenue classifications to small parcels of land is to the disadvantage of the landowners, because it undermines the potential value of the large parcels of land acquired for a single project. Consequently, the uniform valuation for the entire land acquired for the project possesses justification.”

paragraphs.text: Date of hearing 14.10.2026 Appellant(s) by Syed Fayyaz Hussain Zaidi, Advocate with Arslan Binyamin, Advocate. Respondent(s) by Mr. Bashir Ahmad Buzdar, Assistant Advocate General with Mukarram Sultan, AC City Multan and Tehseen, Inspector/Focal Person, CPO, Multan. JAWAD HASSAN, J. This judgment shall decide titled appeal filed under Section 54 of The Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (the “Act”) which is arising from the judgment and decree dated 12.10.2023 (the “impugned judgment”), whereby Senior Civil Judge (Civil Division), Multan (the “Referee Court”) proceeded to dismiss reference application filed by the appellants under Section 18 of the “Act”.

The factual background giving rise to the instant appeal is that the appellants are owners of land measuring 06 Kanals, comprised in Khewat No.369/379, Khatooni No.670 Min, Khasra Nos.46/13/2, 14/1/2 and 14/2, situated in Mouza Bouapur, Tehsil and District Multan. Out of the aforesaid land, an area measuring 05 Kanals, 07 Marlas and 05 Sarsai was acquired by the Commissioner, Multan Division, Multan, at the request of the City Police Officer, Multan, for the construction of Police Station Seetal Mari, Multan. Dissatisfied with the assessment of compensation determined by Respondent No.1, the appellants submitted their objections on 14.12.2019, asserting that the amount assessed was inadequate and unacceptable. Accordingly, they sought a reference to the competent Court under Section 18 of the “Act” for proper adjudication of their claims regarding compensation. Pursuant to their request, the matter was referred to the “Referee Court”, which, after framing the issues and recording the evidence of the parties, adjudicated the reference and rendered the “impugned judgment”, which has been assailed by the appellants through the instant appeal.

Earlier vide judgment dated 14.04.2025, this Court remanded the case to the “Referee Court” which was challenged by the appellants in C.P.No.2691 of 2026 and the Supreme Court of Pakistan vide order dated 21.01.2026 set aside the aforesaid order of this Court and remanded the matter to be decided on merits on the basis of available record.

Learned counsel for the appellants inter alia argued that the “Referee Court” while deciding issue No.1, has failed to consider or discuss the material evidence of Local Commissioner (AW-5), who assessed the prevailing market value of the acquired land at Rs.1.5 to 1.8 million per Marla as per his report (Exh.A2) by referring letter No.331-2012/189(BOR), evidencing acquisition of land in the same locality in 2012 at the rate of Rs.700,000/- per Marla, whereas the appellants’ land was assessed in 2017 at Rs.400,000/- per Marla for commercial land and Rs.250,000/- per Marla for the land situated behind the road; that the “Referee Court” has ignored the evidence of Halqa Patwari (AW-2) who exhibited the site plan (Exh.A1) of the land proposed for construction of Police Station Seetal Mari and said site plan clearly depicts that the acquired land is situated along the main Khanewal Road, with a showroom in its immediate vicinity and as such has resulted in an erroneous determination of the nature and market value of the acquired land; that the acquired land measuring 05 kanals, 07 marlas and 05 sarasi, out of a total holding of 06 kanals, constitutes one contiguous and integrated unit; however, the Land Acquisition Collector arbitrarily divided it into frontage and rear portions and awarded compensation at different rates, without any cogent justification, despite its acquisition for a single public purpose; that the entire land ought to have been assessed uniformly, keeping in view its collective market value and potentiality; that the respondents have failed to produce any evidence to rebut the oral and documentary evidence adduced by the appellants rather they merely tendered the award and relevant acquisition documents, without controverting the appellants’ claim regarding the nature and market value of the acquired land and the claim of the appellants remained unrebutted, which the “Referee Court” has failed to properly appreciate.

Learned Law Officer supported the “impugned judgment” and argued that the “Referee Court” has rightly dismissed the reference of the appellants as they were adequately compensated according to the market value of their land at the spot and the price of land was fixed after observing all legal formalities. He further submitted that the Local Commissioner exaggerated the market value, rendering his assessment contrary to the facts and law.
Arguments heard. Record perused.

We have noticed that the “Referee Court” captured the disputed area of facts by framing following issues: 1. Whether the Award dated 08.01.2020, passed by respondent No.1 is against law and facts and is liable to be cancelled? OPA 2. If the above issue is proved in affirmative, then whether the applicants are entitled to recover compensation to the tune of Rs.25 or 30 lac per marla alongwith compulsory charges and compound charged interest? OPA 3. Whether the petitioners have no cause of action to file the instant reference? OPR 4. Whether the petitioners have not come to the court with clean hands? OPR 5. Whether the Award announced by respondent No.1 is according to law and according to market value, the applicants have been paid full price? OPR 6. Whether the report of local commission is maintainable (an additional issue vide order dated 21.12.2021)? OP Parties. 7. Relief.

The pivotal question requiring determination in the present appeal is whether the compensation assessed for the acquired land reflects its market value, nature, location and potentiality as per provisions of the “Act”. The scheme of the “Act” is predicated upon the cardinal principle that collective welfare prevails over individual interest and private ownership must yield to the sovereign authority of the State when necessity so demands. The “Act” was enacted to provide a comprehensive legal framework for the compulsory acquisition of land required for public purposes coupled with a mechanism for determining just compensation to those dispossessed. Though the “Act” empowers the State to acquire private property through compulsory process yet such authority is neither absolute nor unfettered. It is circumscribed by the fundamental requirement that the acquisition must genuinely serve a public purpose and that the owner is compensated in a manner commensurate with the value of the property acquired. The legislative intent underlying the “Act” is not to burden or oppress citizens but to strike a fair balance between public necessity and private rights. The jurisprudential foundation of the law is that a landowner whose property is compulsorily acquired must receive a just equivalent of what has been taken from him viz; gold for gold, never copper for gold; in other words, the law contemplates compensation equivalent to value of the property acquired and not a substitute of lesser worth. The “Act” constitutes a complete and self-contained code inasmuch as it prescribes the procedure for acquisition, provides the mechanism for measurement and valuation of land, regulates the payment of compensation and furnishes remedies for adjudication of disputes arising therefrom. In interpreting such legislation, the preamble assumes considerable significance. Though it does not form an operative part of the statute yet it serves as a key to understanding the object, purpose and legislative intent behind the enactment. The preamble illuminates the mischief sought to be remedied and the objectives intended to be achieved by the legislature, thereby providing valuable guidance in construing the substantive provisions of the law. Reliance in this regard is placed on DIRECTOR GENERAL, FIA AND OTHERS Versus KAMRAN IQBAL and others (2016 SCMR 447) wherein the Supreme Court of Pakistan has laid down the similar principle by holding that “indeed, preamble to a Statute is not an operative part thereof, however, as is now well laid down that the same provides a useful guide for discovering the purpose and intention of the legislature.

We are mindful of the fact that Section 23 of the “Act” is the principal provision governing the determination of compensation payable to a landowner whose property is compulsorily acquired by the State. The said provision reads as under: “23. Matters to be considered in determining compensation.– (1) In determining the amount of compensation to be awarded for land acquired under this Act, the Court shall take into consideration– Firstly, the market value of the land at the date of the publication of the notification under section 4, sub- section (1); Secondly, the damage sustained by the person interested, by reason of the taking of any standing crops or trees which may be on the land at the time of the Collector's taking possession thereof; Thirdly, the damage (if any) sustained by the person interested, at the time of the Collector's taking possession of the land, by reason of severing such land from his other land; Fourthly, the damage (if any) sustained by the person interested, at the time of the Collector's taking possession of the land, by reason of the acquisition injuriously affecting his other property, moveable or immoveable, in any other manner, or his earnings; Fifthly, if, in consequence of the acquisition of the land by the Collector, the person interested is compelled to change his residence or place of business, the reasonable expenses (if any) incidental to such change; and Sixthly, the damage (if any) bona fide resulting from diminution of the profits of the land between the time of the publication of the declaration under section 6 and the time of the Collector's taking possession of the land. (2) In addition to the market-value of the land as above provided, the Court shall award a sum of fifteen per centum on such market-value, in consideration of the compulsory nature of the acquisition. (3) For the purpose of clause first of sub-clause (1) of this section the market value of the land shall be determined on the basis of the average net income of that land for the five years preceding 1st September, 1961: Provided that if in any of these years that land or any portion of it has not been cultivated, the net income of such land or portion in that year shall be taken to be three times the land revenue assessed thereon, if no land revenue has been so assessed, three times the lowest rate of land revenue assessed on neighboring land; Provided further that in respect of land which is situated in town or village abadi or land which is attached to a house, manufactory, or other building and is reasonably required for the enjoyment and use of the house, manufactory, or building, the market-values shall be the market-value according to the use to which the land was being put on the 1st September, 1961.” The above provision of law embodies the fundamental principle that while the sovereign possesses the power of eminent domain to acquire private property for a public purpose, such acquisition must be accompanied by payment of just, fair and reasonable compensation so that the owner is placed, as nearly as possible, in the same pecuniary position in which he would have stood had his property not been acquired. The object of Section 23 of the “Act” is twofold. Firstly, it provides a comprehensive mechanism for assessing the true value of the property acquired and the consequential losses suffered by the owner. Secondly, it seeks to ensure that the burden of a public project is not disproportionately imposed upon an individual landowner whose property is taken for the benefit of the community at large. This provision, therefore, acts as a safeguard against arbitrary or inadequate compensation and serves to balance public interest with private property rights. Section 23(1) of the “Act” enumerates the matters which the Court is mandatorily required to take into consideration while determining compensation. The first and foremost factor is the market value of the land as it existed on the date of publication of the notification under Section 4(1) of the “Act”. The significance of this clause lies in the fact that the market value must be determined with reference to the date on which the acquisition proceedings commenced and not on the basis of any subsequent increase or decrease in value. The expression “market value” denotes the price which a willing purchaser would reasonably pay to a willing seller in an open and competitive market, having regard to the location, nature, quality, fertility, utility, existing advantages and future potential of the land. Section 23(2) of the “Act” mandates payment of an additional amount over and above the market value of the land on account of the compulsory nature of the acquisition. This statutory addition, commonly known as compulsory acquisition charges or solatium, recognizes that the owner is not a voluntary seller and is being deprived of his property by operation of law. The provision, therefore, compensates the owner for the involuntary character of the transaction and the inconvenience resulting therefrom. Section 23(3) of the “Act” lays down a special method for determination of market value by reference to the average net income of the land during the five years preceding 1st September, 1961. The subsection was introduced to provide an objective criterion for valuation of agricultural land and to prevent speculative or arbitrary assessments. The first proviso addresses situations where the land remained uncultivated during any of the relevant years and prescribes a statutory formula based upon land revenue assessment. The second proviso carves out an exception in respect of urban land, village abadi, and land attached to residential, industrial or commercial buildings, for which market value is to be determined according to the use to which the land was being put.

The scope of Section 23 is extremely wide. The provision is not confined merely to the physical value of the land but extends to all direct and proximate losses suffered by the owner as a consequence of acquisition. The Court, while exercising jurisdiction under Section 23, is under a legal obligation to award compensation that is real, just and equitable. In doing so, it must consider not only the existing condition of the land but also its potential value, developmental prospects, advantageous location, accessibility, fertility, availability of irrigation facilities, commercial utility and all other factors that a prudent purchaser would reasonably take into account in determining its worth.

Before proceeding further, we are guided by the principles already settled by the Supreme Court in a number of cases which reiterates that the determination of compensation under section 23 of the “Act” must be anchored in objective standards, reflecting the price a willing purchaser would pay to a willing seller in an open market transaction free from compulsion. Reliance on mere averages or subjective opinion of the Collector cannot suffice. Instead, contemporaneous transactions of similar or adjoining lands, awards in respect of property situated in the same locality and the potential use to which the land may reasonably be put must all be taken into account. The Court, therefore, places its reliance on following precedents to ensure that the compensation awarded is just, fair, and in consonance with the law.

In the case of "MALIK HADI HUSAIN and others versus LAND ACQUISITION COLLECTOR and another" (PLD 2008 Supreme Court 386), the Supreme Court has declared that the Court while determining the compensation should have to consider the potential and future prospective of land in addition to one year average. Relevant portion from the said judgment is reproduced herein below:- "It needs no reiteration that while determining the amount of compensation, Court is to consider evidence brought on the record by the parties and further Land Acquisition Collector while determining compensation of acquired land has also to consider the potential and future prospective of land in addition to one year average. While determining the value of the land acquired by the Government and the price which willing purchaser would give to the willing seller, only the past sale should not be taken into account but the value of the land with all its potentiality may also be determined by examining other facts. An assessment of the compensation payable for land acquired must take into account several factors, including the nature of the land, its present use and its capacity for a higher potential, its precise location in relation to adjoining land, the use to which neighbouring land has been put and the impact of such use on the land acquired, and so on having regard to all these factors."

Likewise, in “AIR WEAPON COMPLEX through D.G. versus MUHAMMAD ASLAM and others” (2018 SCMR 779), the Supreme Court confirmed that compensation must reflect both current market value and future potential of acquired land and formulated criteria and factors to be taken into consideration qua assessing compensation of acquired land which are as follows: “(a) its market value at the prevalent time and its potential; (b) one year average of sale taken place before publication of notification under section 4 of the Act of the similar land; (c) its likelihood of development and improvement; (d) a willing purchaser would pay to a willing buyer in an open market arms length transaction entered into without any compulsion; (e) loss or injury occurred by severing of acquired land from other property of the land owner; (f) loss or injury by change of residence or place of business and loss of profit; (g) delay in the consummation of acquisition proceedings and; (h) peculiar facts and circumstances of each case."

The term “market value” was defined by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of “LAND ACQUISITION COLLECTOR versus Mst. SURRAYA MAHMOOD JAN” (2015 SCMR 28) and held that “the term market value as employed in section 23 of the Act of 1894 implies the price that a willing purchaser would pay to a willing buyer in an open market arm's length transaction entered into without any compulsion. Such determination must be objective rather than subjective. While undertaking this exercise, contemporaneous transactions of the same, adjoining or adjacent as well as the land in the same vicinity or locality; in dissenting precedents, may be taken into account. An award of compensation a similar, adjacent, adjoining land or in respect of the land acquired in the same vicinity or locality cannot be ignored. The classification of the land in the Revenue Record cannot be the sole criteria for determining its value and its potential i.e. the use of which the said land can be put, must also be a factor. In this behalf, the use of the land in its vicinity needs to be examined." It has been consistently held that in cases of compulsory acquisition for public purposes, landowners are deprived of the utility of their property, while Collectors often rely merely on their own opinion, ordinarily based on the one-year average preceding the notification under section 4 of the “Act”. Such an approach has been disapproved by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of “GOVERNMENT OF PAKISTAN through Military Estate Officer, Abbottabad and another versus GHULAM MUSTAZA and others" (2016 SCMR 1141) and it has been held that determination of compensation must instead be grounded in objective criteria, including contemporaneous transactions, location, and future potentialities, rather than a mechanical reliance on a one-year average.

Recently Division Bench of this Court in the case of “MUHAMMAD YAQOOB KHAN versus PAKISTAN through Secretary Ministry of Defence, (Civil Aviation Division), Govt. of Pakistan and others” has rendered a judgment dated 25.02.2025 (2025 LHC 2275) by outlining salient features of Section 23 of the “Act”; the relevant observations read as under: “24. The scope and object of Section 23 of the Act has continuously remained under consideration before the superior courts of the country. As a nutshell of discussion so far made upon the true import of Section 23 of the Act, its salient features outlined are as under:- (a) market value of land at the prevalent time and its potential; (b) one year average of sale taken place before publication of notification under section 4 of the Act of the similar land; (c) its likelihood of development and improvement; (d) a willing purchaser would pay to a willing buyer in an open market arms length transaction entered into without any compulsion; (e) loss or injury occurred by severing of acquired land from other property of the land owner; (f) loss or injury by change of residence or place of business and loss of profit; (g) delay in the consummation of acquisition proceedings and; (h) peculiar facts and circumstances of each case. 25. Section 23 of the Act, thus, does not restrict or hinge upon a single factor, rather it provides for various matters to be taken into consideration while determining compensation. We are mindful of the fact that initially, there was a trend that while determining the compensation, market value of the land at the date of publication of notification under section 4 of the Act was mainly taken into consideration but with the passage of time, law to this effect has gone under radical change and now the dominant factor is the potential value of the land. Market value is only one of such factors to be considered for the purpose of award of compensation to the landowners. Location, neighborhood, potentiality or other benefits, which may ensue from the land in future could not be ignored. The most dominant and guiding factor would be that the compensation should be determined at the price, which a willing buyer would pay to a seller as per his satisfaction. But at the same time, one cannot lose sight of the fact that compensation cannot be determined and awarded to the landowners as a bounty of state without taking into consideration the above noted salient features”

The above interpretation accorded to Section 23 of the “Act” correctly reflects the legislative intent underlying the provision and provides an appropriate framework for determining fair and just compensation in cases of compulsory acquisition. The learned Division Bench has held that while assessing compensation, the Court is required to determine the true market value of the acquired land by taking into account all relevant factors, including its nature, location, quality, utility, existing advantages and future potential, so as to ensure that the landowner receives a fair equivalent for the property of which he has been deprived. Since the facts and legal controversy involved in the present appeal are substantially governed by the principles laid down in the aforesaid judgment, we respectfully adopt and follow the same and hold that the compensation payable to the appellants is to be determined in accordance with the parameters set forth therein.

We may now examine the evidence adduced in this case in the light of the principles, enumerated above, and make a bid to find out the use, nature and kind of the appellants' land. Undisputedly, out of 06-kanals, land measuring 05 Kanals, 07 Marlas and 05 Sarsai was acquired by the Commissioner, Multan Division, Multan, at the request of the City Police Officer, Multan, for the construction of Police Station Seetal Mari, situated in Mouza Bouapur Tehsil Multan City District Multan. In pursuance thereof, the Land Acquisition Collector, Multan announced award dated 08.01.2020 by assessing market price of land at the rate of Rs.4,00,000/- per malra as residential to the extent of 50 feet front on main Multan Khanewal Road and at the rate of Rs.2,50,000/- per marla as residential for remaining land behind the road. The appellants, being aggrieved and dissatisfied with the quantum of rate assessed by the Land Acquisition Collector on the ground that the same did not represent the true market value of the acquired land prevailing at the relevant time, submitted an application dated 19.02.2020 under Section 18 of the “Act” seeking reference of the dispute to the “Referee Court” for determination of adequate price of acquired land. In the said reference proceedings, the appellants specifically asserted that the acquired land possessed considerable commercial and residential value and therefore, claimed value of the land as Rs.25/30 lac per marla. In support of their claim, the appellants produced both oral as well as documentary evidence. The oral evidence consisted of statements of witnesses AW-1 to AW-7, whereas documentary evidence was tendered and exhibited as Exh.A-1 to Exh.A-5. Through such evidence, the appellants endeavoured to establish the location, nature, fertility, utility and market potential of the acquired land. Conversely, the Respondents contested the claim and, in rebuttal thereof, produced only documentary evidence exhibited as Exh.R-1 to Exh.R-8. The respondents sought to justify the amount determined by the Land Acquisition Collector and disputed the valuation advanced by the appellants. After framing of issues and recording of oral and documentary evidence adduced by both the parties, the “Referee Court” proceeded to dismiss the reference with the following observations I have gone through oral as well as documentary evidence of the petitioners. The claims of the petitioners are that the compensation was inadequately assessed by the Land Acquisition Collector and the price of the land be enhanced. The petitioner in support of her claims submitted Ex.Al to Ex.A5 in support of their version. During cross examination, petitioner/AW-1 stated that in the year 2012, petitioner property (commercial in nature) was acquired/soled against market value of Rs.7,00,000/- per marla and its surrounded property is also commercial in nature as well as value of the said property is not less than Rs.25/30 Lac per marla. During cross examination, petitioner/AW-1 admitted that she did not file any documentary proof in this regard. Furthermore, during cross-examination AW-3 admitted that he is working as property dealer and approximately 6/7 years ago, he sold out petitioner property which was situated beyond the impugned property and petitioner did not attach any proof of sold-out property with this reference. Besides this petitioner did not produce any register sale deed of crucial period, commercial fee receipt neither the vendor or vendee or any attesting witness. The petitioners have failed to substantiate their claim that the property was inadequately assessed and that petitioner are entitled to get enhanced their compensation award. No cogent piece of evidence has been produced. The petitioners were duty bound to produce the Aks Sajra ) عکس شجرا to ascertain and establish that both the properties are located adjacent and they are same in the quality and nature. Although during cross-examination petitioner admitted that she did not file any proof with regard to prove her stance. Mere oral assertion cannot be made bans for enhancement of market price of acquired land. Therefore, keeping in view the oral & documentary evidence produced, the petitioners badly failed to discharge the onus with regard to the land. Therefore, this issue is decided against the petitioners”.

It is observed that the “Referee Court” fell into error by dismissing the claim for enhancement of compensation primarily on the ground that the petitioners had failed to produce documentary evidence in support of the prevailing market value of the acquired land, without properly examining the material available on the record, particularly the report of the Local Commission (Exh.A-2), which remained un-objected to by either party. The said report specifically highlighted the location of the acquired property on Main Khanewal Road, its main frontage, its location in a densely populated area, establishment of Paramount Colony and the commercial markets and developed urban locality in its vicinity, thereby bearing directly upon the location, potentiality and commercial nature of the acquired land. These material factors were relevant to the determination of its prevailing market value and could not have been brushed aside merely because the appellants had not produced sale deeds or other independent documentary evidence. The “Referee Court”, while emphasizing the absence of Aks Shajra and documentary proof of comparable transactions, failed to appreciate that the report of the Local Commission constituted material evidence requiring due consideration, particularly when its factual findings regarding the location and commercial character of the property had remained unchallenged. Although the report of the Local Commission was not, by itself, conclusive as to the precise market value of the acquired land, the “Referee Court” was required to examine its findings in conjunction with the oral and documentary evidence and to record cogent reasons for accepting or discarding them. The failure to undertake such an exercise, coupled with the omission to assess the effect of the location and commercial potential of the acquired land upon its market value, renders the impugned findings legally unsustainable, as the issue of adequacy of compensation could not have been determined by selectively relying upon the deficiencies in the appellants’ evidence while leaving material and relevant evidence unaddressed.

The principal grievance of the appellants is that land acquired in the same locality in year 2012 was assessed at Rs.7,00,000/- per marla whereas in year 2017 the price of land of the appellants was assessed at lower side i.e. Rs.4,00,000/- per marla for the land on front and Rs.2,50,000/- per marla for land situated behind the road but the “Referee Court” failed to properly consider this material aspect while passing the “impugned judgment”. The appellants, upon whom the burden of proof was placed, first examined Mst. Narjis Khatoon as AW-1 and in cross-examination, she stated that in year 2012, the price of land situated on same Mouza was acquired at the rate of Rs.7,00,000/- per marla. Muhammad Munir, Halqa Patwari, Mouza Boapur, Multan City was examined as AW-2 who admitted the site plan (Exh.A1). Local Commission namely Farhan Abbas, Advocate was appeared as witness (AW-5) and stated that the property in question was not agricultural rather it is commercial one.

It is pertinent to observe that the “Referee Court” failed to record any finding on the report of the Local Commissioner, despite having itself framed a specific issue in that regard on 21.12.2021. The report, which directly pertained to the nature and prevailing market value of the acquired land, constituted material evidence requiring due consideration. The omission to discuss and evaluate such evidence, particularly when a specific issue had been framed by the Court itself, reflects non-appreciation of material evidence and renders the findings on the question of compensation legally unsustainable. The evidence on record demonstrates that the Local Commissioner had specifically reported that the acquired land was situated at a prime location near the populated area and possessed considerable commercial value. However, this uncontroverted evidence was ignored without assigning any lawful or cogent reason.

The “Referee Court” further erred in ignoring the potentiality and future commercial significance of the acquired land. The acquired land is situated on Main Khanewal Road in close proximity to a populated area and is surrounded by commercial markets, showrooms, residential colony known as Paramount Society with bazaars situated on opposite side of the road; all of these locational advantages and existing commercial activity in the vicinity were material factors in determining the fair market value of the acquired land. Reliance is placed on “SARHAD DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY N.W.F.P. (Now KPK) through COO/CEO versus NAWAB ALI KHAN and others” (2020 SCMR 265) wherein the Supreme Court affirmed that there is judicial consensus in considering the potential value of property essentially, the future use to which it can be put as well as the escalation in land prices during the period from the publication of the notification under Section 4(1) of the “Act” until the culmination of acquisition proceedings in the pronouncement of the award. Identically, the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the matter of "PROVINCE OF PUNJAB through Land Acquisition Collector and another versus BEGUM AZIZA" (2014 SCMR 75) while discussing the earlier precedent law on the subject held that in determining the quantum of compensation the exercise may also not be restricted to the time of notification but its future value may be taken into account. It has further unambiguously been declared that where the acquisition process spans a period of time, the price escalation occurring during that interval must be factored into the determination of the potential value of the land and the “Referee Court” failure to give effect to this salutary principle. Articles 23 and 24 of the Constitution of Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 197 3 guarantee that no person shall be deprived of property without adequate compensation and as this Court held in “MST. LALARUKH SAQLAIN and others versus Punjab Health Department” (2023 YLR 222), even where land is taken for a public purpose, the person deprived thereof must be given compensation that is adequate, fair, just, and due.

To hold otherwise would be to allow the acquiring authority to benefit from the fortuitous absence of a witness and to render nugatory the statutory entitlement of the landowner to full and just indemnification. In “FEDERATION OF PAKISTAN versus NASIR MUNIR AHMED” (2022 CLC 2072), this Court emphasized that the mode of determining compensation under Section 23 of the “Act” entitles the landowner to compensation beyond mere market value, encompassing all losses and injuries flowing from the acquisition and that oral evidence, where credible and reliable, may also be taken into account.

With regard to the ground agitated by the appellants concerning the bifurcation of the acquired land, measuring 05 kanals, 07 marlas and 05 sarasi out of a total holding of 06 kanals, into frontage and rear portions for the purpose of valuation and award of compensation at different rates, the contention is that the entire acquired land, being one contiguous and integrated unit, ought to have been assessed uniformly, keeping in view its collective market value and potentiality. We when confronted this aspect to the latter, they could not satisfy the Court. The preposition is squarely governed by the principles enunciated by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of “FEDERAL GOVERNMENT OF PAKISTAN through Ministry of Defence Rawalpindi and others versus Mst. ZAKIA BEGUM and others” (PLD 2023 Supreme Court 277) wherein it was emphasised that the determination of compensation for acquired land must take into account its market value and potentiality rather than being governed by artificial classifications or fragmentation of the acquired property. In paragraph 16 of the judgment ibid, the Supreme Court has held as under: “Measuring the land in small parcels, based on ownership and revenue classifications is to the disadvantage of the landowners, because it undermines the potential value particularly when the acquisition is of a large area of land for a single project. In such a situation, the landowners must be given the benefit of the potential value of the entire area being acquired and not just small pieces of land, so as to ensure that the landowners are compensated as per the expected reasonable capacity of land use.”

Further, the Supreme Court of Pakistan in paragraph 17 of the judgment ibid explained why the entire area, and not its parts, is the unit of valuation in a single project acquisition and held that “where land is acquired for one project, the potential value of the entire area being acquired is relevant as the very purpose of the acquisition suggests that the land has future prospects.” Likewise, the review filed by the Federal Government against aforesaid judgment (PLD 2023 Supreme Court 277) was dismissed by the Supreme Court of Pakistan through judgment “FEDERAL GOVERNMENT OF PAKISTAN through Ministry of Defence Rawalpindi and others versus Mst. ZAKIA BEGUM and others” (2023 SCMR 2092) holding as under: “Considering that the land is acquired for a single project, this Court has affirmed the value assigned by the High Court to the acquired land for the reason that the original value as determined by the Collector and the Referee Court was based on revenue classifications which have no relevance for the purposes of calculating compensation. Furthermore, when land is acquired in small parcels, awarding compensation based on revenue classifications to small parcels of land is to the disadvantage of the landowners, because it undermines the potential value of the large parcels of land acquired for a single project. Consequently, the uniform valuation for the entire land acquired for the project possesses justification.”

Moreover, the aforesaid principles find supports from the judgment of the Supreme Court of Pakistan cited in “LAND ACQUISITION COLLECTOR, G.S.C., N.T.D.C. (WAPDA), LAHORE and another versus Mst. SURRAYA MEHMOOD JAN” (2015 SCMR 28) wherein it has categorically been held that determination of compensation under Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, is not to be governed merely by the classification or nature of land reflected in the revenue record; rather, its actual market value, location, neighbourhood and potentiality are the relevant considerations. The Court further held that “the classification of the land in the Revenue Record cannot be the sole criteria for determining its value and its potential i.e. the use of which the said land can be put, must also be a factor. In this behalf, the use of the land in its vicinity needs to be examined.” Likewise, in “NATIONAL COMMAND AUTHORITY, etc. versus ZAHOOR AZAM, etc” (2024 CLC 1) the Court while, dealing with a similar controversy, observed that the acquired land, though forming one compact parcel, had been classified into different categories and subjected to differential rates of compensation without assigning any cogent reasons. Paragraph 29 of the same reads as under: “So far “land owners” in R.F.A No.53 of 2014 are concerned, they were deprived of land measuring 136 Kanal 5 Marla falling in Khasra Nos.1842 to 1850. Their land was though in the compact form as is evident from ‘Aks Shajra Kishtwar’ Exh.A6 but it was also categorized in different kinds as of nature and compensation as well without assigning any reasoning. Land in question is situated in the proximity of other acquired land and cannot be bifurcated. Law does not allow any discrimination amongst the equal. “Land owners” therein are thus also entitled for similar treatment in the matter of compensation”

In view of the foregoing authoritative pronouncements, it is evident that the determination of compensation must be founded upon the collective potentiality and actual market value of the acquired property, rather than an artificial division of one integrated parcel into separate portions. In the instant case, the acquired land constitutes one contiguous unit and was acquired for a single public purpose.

Notably, though the evidence adduced by both parties may not be regarded as conclusive for determining the precise market value of the acquired land, yet the Court cannot lose sight of the cumulative effect of the material available on record. The appellants have not produced sufficient independent documentary evidence, particularly contemporaneous sale deeds, to conclusively establish the exact market value claimed by them. Conversely, the respondents have also failed to produce any cogent material to substantiate that the compensation assessed by the Land Acquisition Collector truly represented the prevailing market value of the acquired property. In such circumstances, the Court is required to undertake a judicial appraisal of the entire record rather than confine itself to the deficiencies in the evidence of either party. The location of the acquired land along Main Khanewal Road, its proximity to established commercial markets, showrooms, a populated locality and Paramount Society, coupled with the report of the Local Commissioner regarding its nature and potential, constitutes relevant material which cannot be disregarded merely because the parties have failed to establish their respective claims with mathematical precision. Accordingly, by considering the cumulative effect of the oral and documentary evidence and in view of the principles governing the determination of compensation under Section 23 of the “Act”, the Court must arrive at a just, fair and reasonable assessment of compensation through judicial determination, without unduly favouring either party or permitting the deficiencies in their respective evidence to defeat the statutory entitlement of the landowners to adequate compensation.

In view thereof, we are of the considered view that the “Referee Court” committed a material irregularity in failing to determine compensation in accordance with the evidence on record. It is by now a settled principle of law that compensation in compulsory acquisition cases must not be illusory or symbolic; rather, it should be fair, just, reasonable and commensurate with the actual worth and potential of the property acquired. The constitutional guarantees embodied in Articles 23 and 24 of the Constitution require that a citizen deprived of his property for a public purpose must receive adequate compensation so as to place him, as nearly as possible, in the same financial position in which he would have remained had the acquisition not taken place.

In view of the foregoing discussion, the evidence available on record and the settled principles laid down by the Supreme Court of Pakistan regarding determination of compensation under Section 23 of the “Act”, we are inclined to allow this appeal and hold that neither the Land Acquisition Collector nor the “Referee Court” assessed the true market value of the acquired land in its correct perspective. The compensation awarded by forums below falls short of this standard. Keeping in view the totality of circumstances, the location and potential of the acquired land, the prevailing market conditions at the relevant time and the judicial precedents referred to hereinabove, we are of the considered opinion that the ends of justice would be adequately met by assessing the entire land at a uniform rate of Rs.5,00,000/- per marla. Compulsory acquisition charges of 15% already awarded under Section 23(2) of the “Act” shall remain intact. No order as to costs.
